title: Unbalanced W-Flow: Unbalanced Wasserstein Drifting under Finite-Batch Marginal Fluctuations

paper.title: Unbalanced W-Flow: Unbalanced Wasserstein Drifting under Finite-Batch Marginal Fluctuations
paper.abstract: Abstract Teacher-free one-step generative models such as W-Flow learn directly from distributional objectives, with the Sinkhorn divergence providing the strongest empirical performance among the energies studied in W-Flow. However, Sinkhorn divergence is based on balanced optimal transport, whose exact marginal constraints can induce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. We introduce UW-Flow , which replaces the balanced Sinkhorn energy with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity. The resulting dynamics retain W-Flow’s cross-minus-self structure, recover the balanced limit, and preserve target identifiability under suitable assumptions. We further characterize the finite-batch velocity error of balanced and unbalanced transport by comparing each minibatch field with its population counterpart. Our analysis identifies conditions under which marginal relaxation yields smaller minibatch-to-population velocity error, and shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation while the corresponding Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) sensitivity remains controlled by local transport geometry. Controlled experiments on fixed-support and continuous two-mode distributions support these predictions. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100, UW-Flow improves generation under matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation and consistent improvements in the class-conditional setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent progress in teacher-free one-step generative modeling has shown that high-quality generators can be learned directly from distributional objectives ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) is a representative example that defines a Wasserstein gradient flow from a distributional energy and trains a one-step generator to follow the resulting particle updates. Among the distributional energies studied in W-Flow, the Sinkhorn divergence ( Genevay et al., 2018 ; Feydy et al., 2019 ) achieves the strongest empirical performance. The Sinkhorn divergence used by W-Flow is built on balanced optimal transport ( Cuturi, 2013 ) , whose coupling must exactly reproduce both input marginals. In practice, however, the corresponding velocity field is estimated from finite minibatches ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2026 ) , whose empirical composition fluctuates from one update to another. Exact marginal matching can therefore force transport between geometrically unrelated regions when, for example, the sampled proportions of different modes do not agree ( Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) . Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) relaxes these hard marginal constraints through soft penalties ( Liero et al., 2018 ; Chizat et al., 2018 ) , allowing the transported marginals to deviate when exact matching would require undesirable transport. Prior work has shown that such marginal relaxation can improve robustness to minibatch composition mismatch ( Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) and outliers ( Balaji et al., 2020 ) . Motivated by this, we introduce UW-Flow , which uses the debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) as its distributional energy, and derive the resulting Wasserstein velocity. In contrast to prior uses of UOT for minibatch objectives ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) , transport maps or couplings ( Yang and Uhler, 2018 ; Choi et al., 2023 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ) , and scalable JKO schemes ( Choi et al., 2024 ) , our formulation uses the debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence as the population energy that directly defines W-Flow’s one-step velocity. In W-Flow, the transport objective directly determines the velocity field used for one-step learning, and thus replacing the balanced Sinkhorn energy changes the underlying population dynamics rather than merely modifying a coupling within a fixed objective. We show that UW-Flow retains the cross-minus-self structure of W-Flow, recovers the balanced dynamics in the hard-marginal limit ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) , and preserves the desired target-identification property under suitable assumptions. Marginal relaxation therefore defines alternative Wasserstein dynamics while retaining the key structural properties required for distribution matching. We next characterize how finite-batch sampling perturbs the velocity fields induced by balanced and unbalanced transport. Specifically, we measure how far each minibatch velocity deviates from its own population counterpart. For balanced Sinkhorn transport, exact marginal preservation imposes an unavoidable finite-batch velocity error. For UW-Flow, we characterize the leading sensitivity to empirical marginal perturbations and identify conditions under which the UOT minibatch-to-population velocity error is smaller than the corresponding balanced error. In particular, for separated matched modes, the balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation, whereas the corresponding UOT sensitivity remains controlled by the local transport geometry. We further test these predictions on fixed-support and continuous two-mode toy distributions by varying batch size, mode separation, and marginal relaxation. We evaluate UW-Flow on MNIST ( LeCun et al., 1998 ) , CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , and ImageNet-100 ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Tian et al., 2020 ) under matched training budgets. The gains are largest in unconditional generation, where multimodal composition mismatch is more substantial, while class-conditional generation also benefits from marginal relaxation.

sections.heading: Wasserstein flows for one-step generation.
sections.text: Wasserstein gradient flows provide generative models with particle velocities induced by a distributional energy. NSGF ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) studies flows driven by the Sinkhorn divergence, while W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) trains a one-step generator to regress onto the resulting particle updates. Optimal transport (OT) has also been used as a training loss ( Genevay et al., 2018 ) , to construct generators ( Rout et al., 2021 ) , and to pair samples for flow matching ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ) . In W-Flow, the velocity is estimated from balanced minibatch couplings rather than population distributions. Because these couplings must match the sampled marginals exactly, fluctuations in regional sample proportions can alter the transport plan ( Fatras et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) and perturb the velocity used as the regression target.

sections.heading: Relaxed transport.
sections.text: Unbalanced transport relaxes exact marginal matching and has been used to improve the robustness of minibatch couplings ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ) . Related approaches use partial transport to limit mismatched minibatch pairings ( Nguyen et al., 2022 ) , learn maps with reweighted marginals ( Choi et al., 2023 ) , incorporate UOT into flow matching ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) , or formulate scalable JKO-based flows ( Choi et al., 2024 ) . We incorporate an unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence into the W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) framework while retaining the target distribution as an equilibrium of the induced velocity field.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis of transport estimates.
sections.text: Prior analyses study empirical entropic OT maps ( Rigollet and Stromme, 2025 ; Goldfeld et al., 2024 ) and minibatch OT objectives ( Fatras et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ) . Fatras et al. (2021) also demonstrate minibatch UOT particle flows, but their concentration and gradient results concern the expected minibatch loss. To our knowledge, none directly compares the minibatch-to-population error of the cross-minus-self velocity under balanced and unbalanced marginal constraints. We make this comparison and identify a separated-mode setting in which the leading unbalanced error is smaller.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced UW-Flow to reduce the sensitivity of W-Flow’s velocity field to finite-batch marginal fluctuations. Our analysis characterizes the minibatch-to-population error and identifies a separated-mode setting in which marginal relaxation improves finite-batch stability. Controlled experiments support this analysis, while results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100 show gains in generation quality under finite transport support.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our stability comparison measures each minibatch field against its own population field. It does not compare the population velocities of UOT and balanced transport or guarantee better generation for arbitrary distributions. We also do not provide a method for selecting τ \tau for a given setting.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools were used in this work only for two supporting tasks: revising the manuscript for clarity and readability, and proofreading the mathematical derivations for typographical and notational errors. The research itself was carried out by the authors. This includes the idea of using the debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence as the energy for W-Flow, the derivation of the UW-Flow velocity and its identifiability property, the finite-batch error analysis of balanced and unbalanced transport. The authors were also solely responsible for designing the experiments, implementing the method, selecting datasets, baselines, and metrics, interpreting the results, and surveying and positioning the related literature. AI tools were not used for any of these tasks. Every AI-suggested edit was checked by the authors, and any change affecting a mathematical expression was verified against the original derivation before being adopted. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work uses only publicly available datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100) and synthetic distributions, and it does not involve human-subject experiments or the collection of personally identifiable information. As with other generative models, models trained with our method may inherit biases present in the training data and could be misused to produce misleading synthetic images. We do not identify ethical concerns beyond those generally associated with generative modeling.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: All theoretical results are stated with their assumptions in the main text, and complete proofs are provided in Appendix. Appendix E also describes the setup of the velocity-error experiments, and Appendix F provides the full training configurations, hyperparameters, and complete results for the generation experiments. All datasets used in this work are publicly available, and we will release our code upon acceptance.

sections.heading: Appendix B Finite-Batch Error of Balanced Sinkhorn Fields
sections.text: This section derives a non-asymptotic lower bound on the velocity MSE of balanced Sinkhorn fields. The key observation is that exact marginal preservation determines the source-averaged velocity through the empirical sample means. However, Sinkhorn divergence is based on balanced optimal transport, whose exact marginal constraints can induce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. We introduce UW-Flow , which replaces the balanced Sinkhorn energy with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity. The resulting dynamics retain W-Flow’s cross-minus-self structure, recover the balanced limit, and preserve target identifiability under suitable assumptions. We further characterize the finite-batch velocity error of balanced and unbalanced transport by comparing each minibatch field with its population counterpart. Our analysis identifies conditions under which marginal relaxation yields smaller minibatch-to-population velocity error, and shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation while the corresponding Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) sensitivity remains controlled by local transport geometry. Controlled experiments on fixed-support and continuous two-mode distributions support these predictions. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100, UW-Flow improves generation under matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation and consistent improvements in the class-conditional setting. 1 Introduction Recent progress in teacher-free one-step generative modeling has shown that high-quality generators can be learned directly from distributional objectives ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) is a representative example that defines a Wasserstein gradient flow from a distributional energy and trains a one-step generator to follow the resulting particle updates. Among the distributional energies studied in W-Flow, the Sinkhorn divergence ( Genevay et al., 2018 ; Feydy et al., 2019 ) achieves the strongest empirical performance. The Sinkhorn divergence used by W-Flow is built on balanced optimal transport ( Cuturi, 2013 ) , whose coupling must exactly reproduce both input marginals. In practice, however, the corresponding velocity field is estimated from finite minibatches ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2026 ) , whose empirical composition fluctuates from one update to another. Exact marginal matching can therefore force transport between geometrically unrelated regions when, for example, the sampled proportions of different modes do not agree ( Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) . Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) relaxes these hard marginal constraints through soft penalties ( Liero et al., 2018 ; Chizat et al., 2018 ) , allowing the transported marginals to deviate when exact matching would require undesirable transport. Prior work has shown that such marginal relaxation can improve robustness to minibatch composition mismatch ( Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) and outliers ( Balaji et al., 2020 ) . Motivated by this, we introduce UW-Flow , which uses the debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) as its distributional energy, and derive the resulting Wasserstein velocity. In contrast to prior uses of UOT for minibatch objectives ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) , transport maps or couplings ( Yang and Uhler, 2018 ; Choi et al., 2023 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ) , and scalable JKO schemes ( Choi et al., 2024 ) , our formulation uses the debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence as the population energy that directly defines W-Flow’s one-step velocity. In W-Flow, the transport objective directly determines the velocity field used for one-step learning, and thus replacing the balanced Sinkhorn energy changes the underlying population dynamics rather than merely modifying a coupling within a fixed objective. We show that UW-Flow retains the cross-minus-self structure of W-Flow, recovers the balanced dynamics in the hard-marginal limit ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) , and preserves the desired target-identification property under suitable assumptions. Marginal relaxation therefore defines alternative Wasserstein dynamics while retaining the key structural properties required for distribution matching. We next characterize how finite-batch sampling perturbs the velocity fields induced by balanced and unbalanced transport. Specifically, we measure how far each minibatch velocity deviates from its own population counterpart. For balanced Sinkhorn transport, exact marginal preservation imposes an unavoidable finite-batch velocity error. For UW-Flow, we characterize the leading sensitivity to empirical marginal perturbations and identify conditions under which the UOT minibatch-to-population velocity error is smaller than the corresponding balanced error. In particular, for separated matched modes, the balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation, whereas the corresponding UOT sensitivity remains controlled by the local transport geometry. We further test these predictions on fixed-support and continuous two-mode toy distributions by varying batch size, mode separation, and marginal relaxation. We evaluate UW-Flow on MNIST ( LeCun et al., 1998 ) , CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , and ImageNet-100 ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Tian et al., 2020 ) under matched training budgets. The gains are largest in unconditional generation, where multimodal composition mismatch is more substantial, while class-conditional generation also benefits from marginal relaxation. 2 Related Work Wasserstein flows for one-step generation. Wasserstein gradient flows provide generative models with particle velocities induced by a distributional energy. NSGF ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) studies flows driven by the Sinkhorn divergence, while W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) trains a one-step generator to regress onto the resulting particle updates. Optimal transport (OT) has also been used as a training loss ( Genevay et al., 2018 ) , to construct generators ( Rout et al., 2021 ) , and to pair samples for flow matching ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ) . In W-Flow, the velocity is estimated from balanced minibatch couplings rather than population distributions. Because these couplings must match the sampled marginals exactly, fluctuations in regional sample proportions can alter the transport plan ( Fatras et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2022 ) and perturb the velocity used as the regression target. Relaxed transport. Unbalanced transport relaxes exact marginal matching and has been used to improve the robustness of minibatch couplings ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ) . Related approaches use partial transport to limit mismatched minibatch pairings ( Nguyen et al., 2022 ) , learn maps with reweighted marginals ( Choi et al., 2023 ) , incorporate UOT into flow matching ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) , or formulate scalable JKO-based flows ( Choi et al., 2024 ) . We incorporate an unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence into the W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) framework while retaining the target distribution as an equilibrium of the induced velocity field. Statistical analysis of transport estimates. Prior analyses study empirical entropic OT maps ( Rigollet and Stromme, 2025 ; Goldfeld et al., 2024 ) and minibatch OT objectives ( Fatras et al., 2019 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ) . Fatras et al. (2021) also demonstrate minibatch UOT particle flows, but their concentration and gradient results concern the expected minibatch loss. Our analysis characterizes the minibatch-to-population error and identifies a separated-mode setting in which marginal relaxation improves finite-batch stability. Controlled experiments support this analysis, while results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100 show gains in generation quality under finite transport support. Limitations. Our stability comparison measures each minibatch field against its own population field. It does not compare the population velocities of UOT and balanced transport or guarantee better generation for arbitrary distributions. We also do not provide a method for selecting τ 	au for a given setting.
